summary: Shannon Gene and host Chris Koerner discuss how to start reselling with free or cheap goods, then use research and reinvestment to move into larger auction lots. They show examples ranging from couches and books to rugs, pressure washers, furniture, vehicle parts and specialist equipment. Their main growth example is Joe, who built a used pressure-washer resale business in Sacramento. The central lesson is to check local demand, item condition, transport and resale prices before bidding; most of the examples still require substantial physical handling.

tactics.name: Research local demand before bidding
steps: Choose the resale venue first, such as eBay, Whatnot, Poshmark or Facebook Marketplace.
Search the category and inspect sold listings rather than relying on active asking prices.
Check what top sellers list and what appears to sell in the local market.
Use an incognito browser session when researching competitor listings, as Shannon suggests.

quote.text: The thing is is trying to find what sells in your market. That's the first one.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Match inventory to an unfair advantage
steps: List practical advantages such as storage, a warehouse, a barn, helpers, repair skills or a useful network.
Choose products that fit those advantages; avoid bulky appliances if there is no space or moving help.
Use product knowledge to focus on a niche where other bidders may have less expertise.

quote.text: And then you match those products to your what your advantages are.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Use image and listing research to investigate obscure lots
steps: Screenshot unclear auction photos and use image research as a starting point.
Treat AI identification and price estimates as leads, not proof.
Call the auction contact to confirm brand, completeness and condition.
Avoid public questions that expose useful research to competing bidders.

quote.text: The great thing about Gov Deals is you can contact these people. You can ask a question.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Start with low-cost items and build experience
steps: Start with free or cheap local goods such as couches or books.
Make small mistakes and learn what sells before committing to expensive lots.
Reinvest as the seller gains knowledge and can evaluate inventory more quickly.

quote.text: Start small, make some mistakes, figure it out. What do you like to sell?
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Create visual listing content that shows the work
steps: Film time-lapse cleaning or preparation with a phone.
Show visible restoration or condition improvements in the listing.
Use the video to stop local marketplace users while they scroll.

quote.text: You're going to show them doing that as well. And that is the first thing people are going to see when they're scrolling through Facebook Marketplace.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Use local listings to clear a consistent furniture lot
steps: Count the inventory and create separate listings for repeatable item types.
Set a low, clear price and include the pickup address and collection hours.
Say that an item is available while it remains listed and avoid spending time replying to repetitive availability messages.
Offer a room set as a bundle where useful, and state whether prices are firm.

quote.text: If you're seeing it here, it's in stock right now. If you message me, is this still available? I will not respond to you.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Check manifests, photos and freight before buying
steps: Get the manifest and calculate the delivered cost per unit.
Compare freight cost with the auction bid before deciding whether the lot is viable.
Inspect item photos for poor stacking, exposed surfaces and likely damage.
Prefer items protected in their boxes when possible.

quote.text: You want to always have a manifest. They tell you exactly what you're going to get.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Use low-margin staples to bring customers into a store
steps: Stock frequently needed goods that local customers have to travel to buy.
Price them near a familiar retailer's price to encourage visits.
Use the visit to expose shoppers to the rest of the store's changing inventory.

quote.text: He's like, 'I sell it the same price Costco does.' And I just bring it in, bring it in, bring it in. It gets them in the store.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Make a home-based liquidation operation welcome locally
steps: Offer neighbours first access to discounted goods.
Let local families buy items so the business is seen as useful to the community.
Manage delivery times and noise so nearby residents are not surprised by trucks.

quote.text: So everybody gets a deal in your neighborhood. Everybody gets a $100 Blackstone.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Sell liquidation as a treasure hunt
steps: Show buyers the unusual deal and invite interest rather than using pressure-heavy sales language.
Offer a clear discount on recognizable products.
Build repeat local buyers by letting them know more stock may arrive.

quote.text: It's like, wow, I got all this stuff. It's amazing. would you I have these Blackstone grills I could sell for half price.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

tactics.name: Avoid emotional bids in efficient markets
steps: Estimate realizable resale value rather than relying on a high reference price.
Subtract buyer fees and likely selling costs before setting a maximum bid.
Walk away if the spread depends on winning at an unrealistic price.

quote.text: someone's going to be bidding with emotion, which is a big mistake.

evidence_quality.rationale: The guest gives concrete auction, sourcing and operating examples and describes specific processes, but most revenue and profit figures are about third parties and are not independently documented. Some figures conflict or are estimates, including Joe's initial pallet cost and the couch-flipping opening claim. Several valuations came from live listings or a ChatGPT estimate rather than completed transactions.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Shannon promotes a free auction guide and a $5 mastermind. Chris promotes TK Owners and reads an ad for GoHighLevel; these promotions are excluded as business ideas.
